newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke says must beware of EMU fudging.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke says must beware of EMU fudging.

text.p: Britain's finance minister on Sunday accused some other members of the European Union of massaging their national accounts to try to qualify to join a single European currency.
In what appeared to be a reference to France and Italy, Clarke spoke in a BBC interview of "taxes that aren't taxes and pension transfers that have reduced borrowing".
He said he would oppose countries using such devices being allowed to join a single currency if it was plain that they only qualified because of them.

But Clarke insisted that the British government's wait-and-see policy towards the single currency had not changed despite a statement last week by Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind that it was "on balance hostile".
Under the EUs Maastricht Treaty, member states can only join a single currency if they meet certain criteria, such as having a budget deficit no greater than three percent of gross domestic product.

Clarke said artificial manoeuvres to meet such criteria would not count. "It is the underlying reality, what we call the structural deficit, that has got to be right and has got to stay that way," he said.
"You have got to take an extremely serioius, strict view of the convergence of the economies."
Clarke did not say which countries he feared were fudging to qualify for EU monetary union, although he specifically excluded Germany from his accusations.

But France will this year cut its budget deficit by transferring 37 billion francs ($6.7 billion) from the pension fund of France Telecom into its state coffers ahead of the company's partial privatisation.
And Italy is levying a special "Euro tax" to raise 12.5 trillion lire, some 0.6 percent of its GDP.
"I don't think Germany would fudge. I am very surprised that allegations are being hurled against the Federal Republic for fudging -- they are pretty open in their public accounting," Clarke said.

A former member of the central council of Germany's Bundesbank central bank said on Sunday he planned a legal challenge in Germany's Federal Court if the country tried to fudge its economic data to qualify for a single currency.

Wilhelm Noelling, writing in Britain's Mail on Sunday newspaper, said: "Since 1995 our country has not fulfilled the apparently vitally important financial criteria. Nor I believe will they be met in 1997 or 1998."
Clarke said it was "not inevitable, but likely" that the launch date for the new Euro currency would be delayed from the planned January 1, 1999.
But he denied that Rifkind had shifted Britain's position decisively away from joining when he spoke of hostility to the idea on Wednesday.
"Neither of us believes for one instant that the government's policy was on the move that day," he said in reference to newspaper headlines about a more sceptical note.

Clarke repeated the line which he and Rifkind made in a statement to Reuters early on Thursday morning -- that they were hostile to a single currency if there was no genuine convergence in the performance of EU economies.
